analysis.one_liner: Bans trucking companies from running lease-purchase programs that leave drivers with debt and no truck.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in September 2025 with one sponsor and one cosponsor, has sat in a House subcommittee with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Some trucking companies lease trucks to their own drivers under contracts where the driver pays to 'buy' the truck while hauling freight for the same company, but the company controls the work, the pay, and the debt. Under these deals, drivers can end up owing money and losing the truck without ever building ownership. This bill orders the Transportation Department to write rules within a year banning such predatory lease-purchase programs and to create a way for drivers to get out of contracts signed after the rules take effect.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers enrolled in or considering lease-purchase deals with the carrier they drive for. The bill targets programs where the carrier controls the driver's work, pay, and debt while the driver builds no equity or is stripped of the equity they accrued, and gives drivers a process to be released from covered contracts [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Secretary of Transportation to issue regulations, within one year of enactment, prohibiting motor carriers under federal jurisdiction from using predatory lease-purchase programs [S2].

Defines a predatory program as one where the carrier controls the driver's work, compensation, and debts, including through recruitment, operational, tax, and finance practices, while the driver accrues no equity or is forced to give up equity in the truck [S2].

Requires the regulations to include a relief process letting drivers out of a lease-purchase agreement if the Secretary finds its terms violated the new rules and the deal was signed after the rules took effect [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers that run lease-purchase programs would have to end or restructure those deals, giving up a source of revenue and labor control. Carriers argue such programs are a path for drivers to become owner-operators; the bill's definition targets the ones where drivers end up with debt and no truck.

drawbacks.text: The ban hinges on a broad, judgment-heavy definition of 'predatory' covering the whole carrier-driver relationship, which could sweep in lease-purchase deals that work as advertised, narrowing access to the one common route drivers have to become owner-operators [S2].
The prohibition only covers carriers subject to federal jurisdiction under subchapter I of chapter 135, so drivers of purely intrastate carriers are not protected by these rules [S2].
Relief applies only to agreements entered into after the rules take effect, so drivers already trapped in current deals get no remedy under this bill [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and well-documented harm — drivers signing 'own your truck' deals that leave them owing money with nothing to show — and its relief process is a concrete remedy. The honest cost is that a broad, case-by-case definition risks catching legitimate programs and that drivers already stuck in bad contracts get no help. Weighing it, the protections outweigh the costs for the drivers the bill covers, but the bill is narrow in reach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2025 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its Highways and Transit subcommittee, where it has sat with no hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Julia Brownley (D-CA) introduced the bill on September 17, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day [S1][S4].
On September 18, 2025, the committee referred the bill to its Subcommittee on Highways and Transit, where no further action has been taken [S4].
The bill has one cosponsor, a Democrat [S3].
Congress is still in session, so the bill technically remains alive but has moved no further than subcommittee referral [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: With no rules issued and no movement in Congress, carriers running lease-purchase programs keep operating under current terms; drivers in those deals remain unprotected.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Carriers using these lease programs, so far

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; both named supporters are Democrats and no Republican has cosponsored, but no one has publicly opposed the bill either [S3].

industries.note: These carriers lease trucks to their own drivers, control the work, pay, and debt, and collect payments even when drivers end up with no equity and no truck. The bill would ban that model for interstate carriers and let covered drivers out of future contracts, costing the carriers a lucrative and controlling arrangement [S2].
Drivers would gain a route to relief from predatory deals and clearer terms if they pursue truck ownership, though legitimate lease-purchase programs could face new scrutiny [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no hearing, and a Republican-run committee that has taken no action, the bill will almost certainly stall in subcommittee unless its provisions are attached to a larger surface transportation or reauthorization bill, which is rare for a measure this new.
